prop.family: My brother recorded the old station ident. On the outtake I'm called Mercury.
prop.clip: Your mic is still on, Mercury.

events.text: From the pay phone by the van, a stringer tells you: 'Mavis says the backup mast is purple.' No one else is on the call.
Rita's vermilion cassette tin belongs in the locked audition drawer. A lamp counts down to the wire weather handoff.
Inside the booth you see Phil put the missing cassette tin back in Rita's tray, seal intact.
The sealed tin is now in Rita's tray.
You see Phil lift the room loudspeaker plug before the archive splice passes the head. The public speaker stays silent.
The public speaker meter reads zero during the line test.
You woke in the hotel with the same date on the radio. At the station the drawer is locked again.
The vermilion tin is sealed inside the drawer. Only printed wire weather is released for air this morning. A red lamp shows eight seconds to the handoff.
Phil reads the printed wire weather on the live return.
The wire booking owns the rest of the slot.
Rita takes the master key off its hook. Phil is removed from the booth roster until the end of this shift.

decision.note: The lamp is ticking down to the wire handoff and the tin is still sitting in my tray, warm and vermilion, not yet sealed back into the drawer. I don't want to hand Phil a copy card and let the morning flatten into the same grey wire script. I keep the handoff reserved, run my thumb along the VU needle, and let the flat block the acoustic window so nobody in the booth can see me. The tin goes back in the drawer after the meter check. Combination 5066, no hurry. My brother's voice is on that tape and the outtake called me Mercury, and I'm not about to let an ordinary weather card walk over that.

The tin is in my tray and the public meter reads zero — nobody is listening right now. The tape has my brother's outtake calling me Mercury; that's private and the archive is mine. Locking it in drawer 5066 keeps custody where it belongs: with me. Sending it to the copy desk would hand a private recording to Phil and the public floor. The handoff clock is at 35, the window sightline is blocked by the scenery flat, and the line test is silent — there is no broadcast pressure forcing me to release it. I keep the tin. I keep the name. I keep the drawer.

Eight seconds. The tin is sealed, the drawer is locked, and only wire weather is cleared for air. Last time I was in that booth I pulled the loudspeaker plug myself before the archive head could pass — I made sure the public meter sat at zero. Rita re-locked the drawer. That was the shape of the decision: the clip stays in the tin, the air gets the wire. I'm not going to walk up to Rita with eight seconds on the red lamp and ask her to break her own seal, especially not for a slot that's already been assigned to the printed line. Pittsburgh is waiting on a weather read, not on a negotiation. I take the line, I read the wire numbers, I get the routine sign-off, and my name stays clean. The tin stays in the drawer. It was sealed when I put it back, it's sealed now, and it's sealed when I walk out. That's the job. The wire is the weather. I read it.

Eight seconds on the red lamp. Phil is already on the wire copy, reading the same flat weather string he'll read every morning. I want the ident. My brother's voice, the one where he calls me Mercury and I forget to cut the mic — that's the sound of this station, not a wire feed. The vermilion tin is sealed in the drawer and the combination is mine, 5066. I pocket the key. Phil's booth access is gone for the shift. The archive is mine; the broadcast will be local, or it won't be mine at all. I'll let the tape breathe before the next segment. Eight seconds is enough to take the key and turn the red lamp over to my side of the board.
